intro: The third movement of Mahler’s Symphony No. 4, Ruhevoll (Poco adagio), is a set of variations on a long G-major melody, which the cellos play above plucked bass notes. An oboe introduces a second tune, and near the end the full orchestra moves suddenly to E major.

sections.label: A · G-major melody, cellos over plucked basses
sections.mNote: A G-major melody over sustained violas

sections.label: B · Oboe theme in E minor
sections.mNote: A slower theme marked plaintive and very expressive

sections.label: A′ · Opening theme varied, clarinets and violas
sections.mNote: The opening melody returns in shorter note values.

sections.label: B′ · Cor anglais joins the lament
sections.mNote: The sorrowing melody returns in G minor

sections.label: A″ · Cello theme varied, quicker tempi
sections.mNote: The Andante gives way to sudden quick variations.

sections.label: Coda · E major, full orchestra
sections.mNote: Strings and harp, then a broad tune in the brass

cues.title: Cello melody in G major
cues.text: Divided cellos play a melody in G major above a pizzicato bass line. The violas hold the harmony, and the violins and winds rest. Mahler marks the cello melody sehr gesangvoll (very songful).
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 4, full score, printed p. 304: divided cellos, sustained violas and pizzicato basses. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/40/IMSLP70999-PMLP58739-Mahler_-_Symphony_No._4_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Opening theme, pizzicato basses
cues.text: Under the cellos’ melody the double basses play the same slow steps pizzicato, over and over. The Mahler Foundation describes the opening theme as “motionless and meditative with its passacaglia bass”.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation page on the movement describes the opening theme with its passacaglia bass: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-4/symphony-no-4-movement-3-ruhevoll-poco-adagio/ . Full score, printed p. 304: double basses pizzicato.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Oboe line above the violins
cues.text: The melody rises into the violins. Above it an oboe plays an independent line, marked zart, tender. The basses continue pizzicato beneath.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 304, rehearsal 1: oboe marked zart above the violin melody; pizzicato bass line continues.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mahler’s description, 1901
cues.text: In 1901 Mahler described this Adagio. St Ursula presides over it with a smile, like the smile on the stone knights and prelates lying in churches with their hands joined. Its character, he wrote, is “solemn, blessed peace; serious, gentle gaiety”.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s introduction to the symphony quotes Mahler’s 1901 description of the Adagio: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-4/symphony-no-4-introduction/

cues.title: Mahler’s recollection of his mother
cues.text: While he wrote this movement, Mahler sometimes glimpsed his own mother’s face “smiling through her tears”. It was, he recalled, the face of a woman who had been able to solve and forgive all suffering by love.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s introduction to the symphony reports this recollection of the composition: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-4/symphony-no-4-introduction/

cues.title: Bruno Walter’s letter, December 1901
cues.text: Bruno Walter proposed “Saint Ursula Laughs As Well” as a possible title for this movement, explaining that the saint’s solemn face carried a smile. He wrote the letter at Mahler’s request in December 1901.
cues.evidence: Walter to Ludwig Schiedermair, 5 December 1901, quoted and discussed by Bettie Jo Basinger: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

cues.title: Second theme, oboe, E minor
cues.text: At rehearsal 2 the tempo becomes much slower (Viel langsamer). An oboe plays the second theme in E minor, marked klagend, sehr ausdrucksvoll, with bassoon and horn accompanying. The violins then take over the tune and lead to a climax with brass.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 306–308, rehearsal 2: Viel langsamer, oboe klagend, sehr ausdrucksvoll, bassoon and horn accompaniment, then violins singend. E-minor second theme: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Fliessend, then Etwas drängend
cues.text: The tempo quickens to Fliessend (flowing) over pizzicato cellos and basses. A page later Mahler marks Etwas drängend. Leidenschaftlich (somewhat pressing, passionately). Flutes, oboes, clarinets and bassoons rise to fortissimo over a rising bass.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 307: Fliessend with pizzicato cellos and basses, then a tempo, Etwas drängend. Leidenschaftlich and fortissimo woodwinds with a rising bass: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/40/IMSLP70999-PMLP58739-Mahler_-_Symphony_No._4_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Bells raised, first outburst
cues.text: Oboes, clarinets, horns and trumpets raise their bells (Schalltrichter auf) for the movement’s first great outburst, over a timpani roll. Etwas zurückhaltend and Wieder langsam then restore the slow tempo at once.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 308: Schalltrichter auf in the woodwinds, horns and trumpets at fortissimo, with timpani; Etwas zurückhaltend, Rit., Wieder langsam: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/40/IMSLP70999-PMLP58739-Mahler_-_Symphony_No._4_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Opening melody, clarinets and violas
cues.text: Clarinets and violas play the opening melody again in quicker notes, with pizzicato cellos and double basses underneath. Mahler marks the passage Anmuthig bewegt (graceful motion). It begins very moderately and gets gradually faster.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 309, rehearsal 4: Anmuthig bewegt, clarinet and viola melody, pizzicato cellos and basses; instruction to begin very moderately and move gradually faster.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Aussee, summer 1899
cues.text: In summer 1899 Mahler rented a villa at Aussee within earshot of the bandstand; it was cold and wet. Discouraged, he picked up a book, and ideas followed. He drafted the first three movements in about ten days and left the sketches in a desk drawer until the next summer.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s introduction describes the weather, the villa near the bandstand and the sketches left in a drawer: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-4/symphony-no-4-introduction/ . Bettie Jo Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide gives about ten days for the first three movements: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

cues.title: Return of the lament in G minor
cues.text: The lament returns in G minor, shared by oboe and cor anglais. Their lines overlap above quiet horns. The return is brief at first; the strings then take up the tune and carry it to a larger outburst.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 314, rehearsal 6: Langsam, oboe and cor anglais with horns. G-minor return and its expansion: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Climax at rehearsal 7
cues.text: The lament rises to a sustained fortissimo, with the strings at full force and the woodwinds playing with bells raised. Basinger calls this the tragic climax of the variation. The harmony modulates through many keys.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 315, rehearsal 7: fortissimo strings and Schalltrichter auf in the woodwinds: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/40/IMSLP70999-PMLP58739-Mahler_-_Symphony_No._4_(orch._score).pdf . Basinger names the tragic climax: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . The Mahler Foundation calls the tonality of this section unstable, modulating through many keys: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-4/symphony-no-4-movement-3-ruhevoll-poco-adagio/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Diminuendo to pppp
cues.text: The music is marked Zurückhaltend, molto dim. and morendo. The instruments drop out one by one, and the timpani and strings reach pppp. Then the cellos bring back the opening tune.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 318: Zurückhaltend, molto dim., morendo and pppp in the timpani and strings: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/40/IMSLP70999-PMLP58739-Mahler_-_Symphony_No._4_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Allegretto in 3/8 and variations
cues.text: The cellos play the opening tune again over pizzicato violas and basses. The metre then changes suddenly to 3/8 and the strings begin an Allegretto. The variations that follow grow faster until Mahler returns to the slow melody.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 319, rehearsal 9: Andante, then Allegretto subito in 3/8 with an explicit instruction to change tempo suddenly; the following variations accelerate before Andante returns.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Allegro subito, rehearsal 10
cues.text: Mahler’s score says each change of tempo comes “just as suddenly and surprisingly as before” (ebenso plötzlich und überraschend wie vorhin). Three increases in speed follow. The second restores a two-beat pulse.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 320, rehearsal 10: Allegro subito. Der Tempowechsel vollzieht sich ebenso plötzlich und überraschend wie vorhin: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/40/IMSLP70999-PMLP58739-Mahler_-_Symphony_No._4_(orch._score).pdf . Basinger describes three graduated increases in tempo, the second restoring a two-beat feel: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Allegro molto, then Andante subito
cues.text: At Allegro molto the variation reaches full speed, with piccolo and glockenspiel above fast violins. The opening tempo of the variation then returns, ganz plötzlich.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 322: Allegro molto (subito) with piccolo, glockenspiel and spiccato strings, then Andante subito. Ganz plötzlich das Anfangstempo der Variation: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/40/IMSLP70999-PMLP58739-Mahler_-_Symphony_No._4_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the slow tempo
cues.text: The slow opening tempo returns for two minutes, marked Poco adagio and then Wieder a tempo (Ruhig). Divided strings play zart (tenderly) in long notes held across the bar lines.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 323: Poco adagio, Zart and Wieder a tempo (Ruhig) with divided strings: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/40/IMSLP70999-PMLP58739-Mahler_-_Symphony_No._4_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First read-through, 12 October 1901
cues.text: At the first read-through of the symphony, on 12 October 1901, Mahler told Natalie Bauer-Lechner that its first three movements held “the cheerfulness of a higher world, strange to us, that has something eerie and dreadful about it for us”.
cues.evidence: Natalie Bauer-Lechner, Erinnerungen an Gustav Mahler (Leipzig: E. P. Tal, 1923), p. 171, entry “Leseprobe am 12. Oktober 1901”: “die Heiterkeit einer höheren, uns fremden Welt … die für uns etwas Schauerlich-Grauenvolles hat”. Translation ours. https://archive.org/details/erinnerungengust00baue . Bettie Jo Basinger quotes the same remark: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

cues.title: E major outburst, rehearsal 12
cues.text: After the quiet return, the music moves to E major, with running strings, harp and timpani. Horns and trumpets play a broad melody from the finale, a movement before the soprano sings it.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 324–326, rehearsal 12 onwards: E-major outburst, running strings and harp, then Pesante brass melody. Its relation to the finale is described at https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Georg Göhler
cues.text: Mahler wrote to the critic Georg Göhler, faulting him for overlooking the symphony’s thematic connections. Each of the first three movements, he said, is joined to the last “in a most intimate and meaningful way”. The coda of this movement announces the principal motif of the finale.
cues.evidence: Bettie Jo Basinger quotes Mahler’s letter to Georg Göhler about the thematic connections: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . The Mahler Foundation says the coda announces the principal motif of the final movement: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-4/symphony-no-4-movement-3-ruhevoll-poco-adagio/

cues.title: Closing bars, violin harmonics
cues.text: The full brass has stopped. Violins divide into four parts and play high harmonics above soft winds and harp. The final marking is Gänzlich ersterbend — dying away completely.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 327, final system: divided first violins in harmonics and Gänzlich ersterbend.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First performance, Munich, 1901
cues.text: Mahler conducted the first performance in Munich on 25 November 1901, with the soprano Margarethe Michalek. The audience had expected another titanic symphony and was baffled by the Fourth’s innocence. The performance was roundly booed.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s concert record names the venue, orchestra and soloist: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/locations/germany/munich/1901-concert-munich-25-11-1901/ . Its introduction describes the audience’s reaction: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-4/symphony-no-4-introduction/

transitions.title: Oboe entry in E minor
transitions.from: A · G-major melody, cellos over plucked basses
transitions.to: B · Oboe theme in E minor
transitions.how: The G-major music slows and dies away, marked morendo, in muted strings and held wind chords. At rehearsal 2, Viel langsamer, an oboe begins an E-minor melody over bassoon and horn. The strings rest and are marked Dämpfer ab to remove their mutes.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed p. 306, rehearsal 2: morendo, Viel langsamer, oboe entry and Dämpfer ab in the resting strings.

transitions.title: Plucked strings bring back the first theme
transitions.from: B · Oboe theme in E minor
transitions.to: A′ · Opening theme varied, clarinets and violas
transitions.how: The closing phrases of the lament die away. At rehearsal 4, marked Anmuthig bewegt, clarinets and violas return to the first theme over plucked cellos and basses. Mahler kept the underlying beat at first, then directed that the variation become gradually livelier.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed p. 309, rehearsal 4 and its tempo instruction.

transitions.title: Oboe and cor anglais in G minor
transitions.from: A′ · Opening theme varied, clarinets and violas
transitions.to: B′ · Cor anglais joins the lament
transitions.how: The variation of the first theme closes with a phrase for solo violin over quiet horns. At rehearsal 6 an oboe pickup starts the lament again. At Langsam the cor anglais, marked klagend, joins the oboe in G minor. The strings stop, and the two reeds play over soft horn chords.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed p. 314, rehearsal 6: oboe pickup, cor anglais klagend and horn accompaniment.

transitions.title: Cellos return to the first theme
transitions.from: B′ · Cor anglais joins the lament
transitions.to: A″ · Cello theme varied, quicker tempi
transitions.how: The second lament falls away to pppp. The cellos begin the first theme at Andante, and the violas and double basses play pizzicato beneath them. The clarinets enter later, before the abrupt change to the faster variation in three time.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 318–319, rehearsal 9 and the subsequent Allegretto subito.

transitions.title: Luftpause, then E major
transitions.from: A″ · Cello theme varied, quicker tempi
transitions.how: The slow theme ends on soft, sustained chords. A Luftpause before rehearsal 12 separates them from the sudden E-major outburst, marked by a change of key signature. Strings run up and down, harp arpeggios cross the orchestra and timpani reinforce the bass. Horns and trumpets then play the finale’s broad melody, marked Pesante.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 324–326: Luftpause before rehearsal 12, E-major key signature, then the Pesante brass phrase.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 4, III. Ruhevoll (Poco adagio), full score (IMSLP70999)
source.locator: Third movement, printed pp. 304–327, rehearsal figures 1–13: cello theme, oboe lament, variations and E-major coda.

timeline.note: The cellos, divided in two groups, play the theme over sustained violas and pizzicato basses; the violins and winds are silent.
An oboe adds a quiet countermelody as the violins take over the cello tune.
The violins are divided and play high; bassoons and horns support them, and the harp adds a few notes.
An oboe plays the E-minor lament over bassoon and horn; the strings rest and remove their mutes.
The violins play the lament while the lower strings and winds move beneath them.
Woodwinds rise to fortissimo over tremolo strings and an ascending bass line.
Horns and trumpets, with bells raised, bring the lament to its first brass climax; the timpani roll beneath.
Clarinets and violas play the livelier theme over plucked cellos and basses.
Cor anglais and oboe play the lament; horns and low strings add soft harmony.
Full strings, wind chords and horns carry the lament forwards over rolling timpani.
Clarinets, horns and soft timpani die away with the strings to pppp.
A bowed cello melody begins the final variation over plucked violas and basses; the clarinets rest and join later.
Violins and violas play figures in the three-beat Allegretto, which begins suddenly.
Rapid violin figures, piccolo and glockenspiel mark the Allegro molto.
Divided strings play the slow theme above soft horns and clarinets.
The music moves into E major, with rolling strings, harp glissandi and a full wind and timpani tutti.
Horns and trumpets raise their bells for the broad melody, marked Pesante.
Harp and divided strings return, very softly, above quiet winds and horns.
Violins in four parts play harmonics high above soft winds and harp.

composer.epithet: Conductor who composed during the summers and intended each symphony to contain a whole world, combining the sublime with the music of the street band.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. In Iglau he heard bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church, and these sounds recur throughout his music. Late in life he told Sigmund Freud that he had once run from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was playing Ach, du lieber Augustin.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, where he studied piano and composition, and he sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. Among his friends were Hugo Wolf and Hans Rott, who died young. Rott’s symphony is so close to Mahler’s own music that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. By then he had already begun his career as a conductor.
